title.en: Chalukyas, Pallavas and the rise of the Cholas (additional, not in the textbook)

text.en:
On a visit to Mahabalipuram, Kavya saw a temple carved out of rock facing the sea.
"Who built this?" she asked. "The Pallavas, about 1300 years ago," said the guide.

After the Guptas, India had many regional kingdoms. In the south the Chalukyas ruled from Badami and the Pallavas ruled from Kanchipuram. Harsha ruled in the north from Kannauj, and the Palas ruled Bengal and Bihar.
The Pallavas built the shore temple and rock-cut shrines at Mahabalipuram. The Chalukyas built temples at Aihole and Pattadakal. The Rashtrakutas carved the Kailasa temple at Ellora. The Palas supported the university at Nalanda.
In the 9th century the Cholas began to rise in the Kaveri delta. Kingdoms often fought each other, but they also gave gifts to temples, supported scholars and encouraged trade.
After the Guptas, many regional kingdoms ruled India.
The Pallavas built the shore temple at Mahabalipuram.
The Chalukyas ruled from Badami. The Rashtrakutas carved Kailasa at Ellora.
In the 9th century the Cholas began to rise.

problem.en: How do temples help us learn about kingdoms?

text.en: Temples carry inscriptions with the names of kings and gifts.
Their carvings show the art and skills of the time.
So temples are sources of history.

prompt.en: A friend says only battles matter in history. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: Kings also built temples and supported learning.
Art and inscriptions tell us about the past.

points.en: Regional kingdoms such as the Pallavas and Chalukyas rose after the Guptas.
The Cholas began to rise in the 9th century.
